title: Surfaces: Classification, Search, Simplification
notes: Open the lecture as a computational version of the surface chapter rather than as a catalog of pictures. The source span moves from intrinsic two-manifold language to triangulated search, then to spatial self-intersections and simplification. Emphasize that each stage keeps a different invariant under control: local disk structure, orientability, Euler characteristic, embedding behavior, and topological type under contractions.

title: Local Surface Model
notes: Use the disk and half-disk models to separate the abstract surface from any drawing in three-space. Interior points must have disk neighborhoods, boundary points have half-disk neighborhoods, and in a triangulation the same condition becomes a statement about vertex links. The computational habit is to test local neighborhoods before trusting any global classification.

title: Example Gallery
notes: Treat the gallery as a feature table, not as a set of decorative shapes. The sphere and torus are closed and orientable, the cylinder has boundary, and the Mobius strip and projective-plane family show why embedded intuition can fail. Ask students to read each example through the three columns: boundary, orientability, and Euler characteristic.

title: Orientability
notes: Orientability is best taught as a transport test. Move a small oriented frame around a closed curve and ask whether it returns with the same sense. In a triangulation, the same idea becomes an edge-by-edge consistency problem: adjacent triangles must induce opposite directions on their shared edge. A failed return is a certificate, not a vague visual impression.

title: Classification Map
notes: Present classification as a decision map whose inputs are compactness, boundary, orientability, and genus. For closed connected surfaces, the orientable branch is the sphere with handles, while the non-orientable branch is the sphere with cross-caps. Boundary components are then made by removing disks from one of those closed models.

title: Polygonal Schemas
notes: Polygonal schemas are finite encodings of a surface, so the slide should feel like data rather than paper folding. Edge labels and directions specify which boundary arcs are identified. The standard orientable schema pairs commutators, while the non-orientable schema pairs same-direction edges. Later algorithms replace this symbolic boundary data with triangle adjacency data.

title: Euler Characteristic
notes: Keep Euler characteristic tied to both counting and classification. For any finite triangulation of a fixed surface, n minus m plus ell is unchanged, so the number survives refinement. Handles reduce chi by two, cross-caps reduce chi by one, and boundary components can be counted separately when the closed-surface formulas are extended.

title: Triangulation Validity
notes: This slide is the local quality gate for every later algorithm. A valid surface triangulation does more than put two triangles on each edge; every vertex link must look like a circle for a closed surface, or an interval at boundary. The invalid cases explain why edge counts alone cannot certify a two-manifold.

title: Ordered Triangle Data Structure
notes: Introduce ordered triangles as a tiny navigation algebra. A triangle has six ordered versions, split into two cyclic orientations. The enext operation advances the lead edge, sym reverses the lead edge, org reads the lead vertex, and fnext crosses to the neighboring triangle across that directed edge. These four moves make surface traversal mechanical.

title: DFS Orientation Algorithm
notes: Explain the algorithm as depth-first search with orientation assignments attached to first visits. When a triangle is reached for the first time, it receives the orientation forced by the incoming edge. When an already marked triangle is revisited, the stored orientation is checked against the incoming one. One contradiction is enough to prove non-orientability.

title: Computing Genus
notes: After orientability is known, genus is just arithmetic on the DFS counts. In a closed triangulated surface, every triangle contributes three edge incidences and every edge is counted twice, so 3 ell equals 2 m. Combining that relation with Euler characteristic gives the two formulas shown, one for the orientable branch and one for the non-orientable branch.

title: Embeddings And Immersions
notes: Shift from intrinsic topology to mappings into R3. An immersion keeps rank two locally, while an embedding is also one-to-one onto its image. Generic smooth maps exhibit double points, triple points, and branch points. The pedagogical distinction is that some self-intersections are accidents of the map, while others are forced by the surface type or by the chosen model.

title: PL Self-Intersection Tests
notes: For a piecewise-linear surface, self-intersection recognition becomes a finite orientation test. The determinant sign says on which side of a triangle plane a point lies. An edge stabs a triangle only when endpoints lie on opposite sides and the directed side tests agree. Two triangle crossings are then classified by which edges perform the stabs.

title: Preimages Of Intersection Curves
notes: The important move is to trace an intersection curve in space and simultaneously trace its preimage on the surface. A spatial path gives two arcs with common endpoints, a closed curve can give two loops, and the most revealing case is one loop covering the image twice. That double cover signals orientation reversal and therefore non-orientable behavior.

title: Edge Contraction And Link Condition
notes: Surface simplification is allowed only when the contraction preserves topology. Contracting edge ab removes the two incident triangles and merges endpoints, but this is safe exactly when the common part of the endpoint links is the edge link itself. Extra shared vertices or edges create non-manifold incidences after contraction, so the link condition is a local topological certificate.

title: Quadric Error And Recap
notes: Close by pairing the topological gate with the geometric priority. The quadric error stores squared distances to the original incident planes, so each candidate contraction asks where the merged vertex should be placed and how much geometric damage remains. The recap should leave students with the chapter workflow: classify the surface, traverse the triangulation, inspect self-intersections, and simplify only when topology and geometry both pass.
